title: Giants DO Exist (Tom Haviland)
summary: Lifter profile of enhanced 6'8" strongman/hybrid athlete Tom Haviland: his twice-a-day 'tactical hypertrophy' program by Josh Bryant, his 7000 kcal clean bulk, neck and isolation training, and a graded physique critique. NH draws lessons for naturals on recovery-driven programming, tall lifters' patience, and small doses of low-rep work for hypertrophy.
claims: He normally skips enhanced lifters because there is little for naturals to learn, but Haviland is an exception: no amount of drugs alone makes someone like him; it takes freak genetics, discipline and excellent programming
PED users who claim drugs do little are mostly coping to avoid admitting much of their success comes from drugs
Haviland: 6'8", 350-400 lb at around 10% bodyfat, 1000 lb frame carry, 700 lb Zercher squat, 660 lb bench
On hypertrophy days Haviland uses bodybuilding methods: dumbbell bench with very slow tempo for 6-10, then cable flies 10-15; it's about using the muscle, not moving the most weight
A good leg day: heavy quad-dominant compound (e.g. squat 6-10) then something for the posterior chain like leg curls, and you're done
A back day only needs one horizontal pull plus one vertical pull
If your bodyweight strength suffers it is usually because body composition is suffering (too much fat); Haviland can do weighted chins and dips at 400 lb because his mass is lean
Haviland's week: 10 sessions, twice a day with two rest days, split across dynamic strength, static strength, hypertrophy and conditioning
Order qualities within a day: dynamic/explosive work before static heavy work, and heavy work before hypertrophy work, to perform when needed while managing fatigue
Splitting heavy work and hypertrophy accessories into separate sessions the same day lets you lift more and get more volume, but doing both in one session is perfectly fine for most
Mindset (from Josh Bryant): ask how much you need to hit the adaptation and what you can realistically recover from, not how little (HIT mindset) or how much (more-is-better)
Never decide set counts arbitrarily: do the amount of sets required to grow, not less and not more; let training dictate recovery choices
Studies show people can go up to 52 sets and see better results, so 'how much can I do' leads to doing far too much
Haviland's bulk day: about 7000 kcal, 361 g protein, ~1000 g carbs, 120 g fat from clean whole foods (beef, rice, sweet potato, veg, eggs, shakes)
Typical lifter on a bulk eats around 3000 kcal
He gains weight easily from just an extra bowl of rice due to a slow metabolism
Tall lifters need much more mass to look impressive and their legs look thin even with good numbers; they tend to dirty bulk, but mostly gain fat. Slow, patient bulking works for them
Tall naturals who are patient end up with higher absolute strength and more impressive presence than shorter lifters; don't give up because you're over 6 feet
Haviland trains neck for hypertrophy (higher reps, full ROM) and isometrically (dragging a sled with a neck harness), which carries over better to contact sports
Everyone should train neck: it looks better and a thick neck can save your life in a car accident; neck grows fast with little time
Strong lifters who disdain isolation work are coping; Haviland trains biceps with full intensity and his arms may be his best body part
Treating every muscle group seriously produces a balanced physique
Big-three lifts should be a way to express strength, not a pigeonhole, unless you compete in them
Low-rep sets (3-5) can help bodybuilders by raising absolute intensity, which helps progression on higher-rep work; disagrees that anything under 5 reps is garbage for hypertrophy
E.g. if you bench only 6-10, add a 3x3 paused or close-grip day to spike intensity; keep sub-5-rep sets around 5% of total program volume
He personally does weighted dips and pull-ups for 3 sets of 3-5 each week and it makes progressing other presses and pulls easier
Don't do one all-out 3RM; in a 3x3 only the last set is near failure through accumulated fatigue. 5x5 is too much; 2x3 or 2x5 may be better for hypertrophy
Online standards are distorted: a natural at 220 lb lean is big in real life; average gym-goer is 170-180 lb and most 200+ lb guys are fat or very tall
Reaching ~200 lb relatively lean as a natural means you look like you lift; this perspective helps fight body dysmorphia
Physique grades for Haviland: S biceps, shoulders, traps, neck, lower back, core, calves; A triceps, forearms, upper back/lats; B quads and hamstrings (curse of long legs)
Short lifters always have an advantage in bodybuilding because it rewards complete proportions, not sheer size
Strongman carries build traps, rounded shoulders and calves
Most men couldn't pick 225 lb up from the floor; Haviland Zercher-cleans and racks about twice that, and does slow 240 lb preacher curl negatives
exercises: triceps; bodyweight strength reflects body comp
isometric, neck fixed, push with head
helps progress other presses and pulls
